title: The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea
gist: The Houthis' capture of Mocha and advance along the Bab al-Mandab coast is the most consequential territorial shift in Yemen in years, giving Iran and its allies leverage over two chokepoints at once — Bab al-Mandab and Hormuz. Chatham House argues the Houthis will pursue 'controlled escalation' to convert military gains into economic leverage, while Trump is caught between defending Saudi Arabia and preserving the May 2025 US–Houthi truce.

insights.claim: With the Houthis holding Mocha and the Bab al-Mandab coastline while Iran disrupts the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and its allies now have the capacity to pressure two of the world's most strategically important maritime chokepoints simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Correlated chokepoint risk means Red Sea and Gulf shipping/insurance premia can no longer be hedged as independent exposures; tail risk to tanker rates and Suez volumes is now joint, not diversified.
insights.quote: Iran and its allies now have the capacity to exert pressure on two of the world’s most strategically important maritime chokepoints.
insights.locator: Together with Iran’s disruption of the Strait

insights.claim: The Houthi capture of Mocha, surrounding areas and nearby islands represents the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years and risks reopening a war that had become significantly less violent since the UN-mediated truce of 2022.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A four-year period of relative calm that markets had priced as the baseline is breaking; reprice Yemen-linked security risk rather than extrapolating the post-2022 truce.
insights.quote: This represents the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years.

insights.claim: The Houthis' likely strategy is controlled escalation — converting military momentum into political and economic leverage without provoking an international response large enough to reverse their gains.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect persistent, calibrated disruption and rent extraction rather than a full closure of Bab al-Mandab — a grinding cost, not a single shock, is the base case.
insights.quote: converting military momentum into political and economic leverage without provoking an international response large enough to reverse their gains

themes.theme: Shipping tolls and spillover to non-Saudi cargo

insights.claim: Houthi assurances that they will not impose formal transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab should be treated cautiously, because there are indications they have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage since beginning attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A de facto private toll regime on Bab al-Mandab is already operating; watch for it to be formalized, which would permanently raise the cost base for Suez routing versus the Cape of Good Hope.
insights.quote: These assurances should be treated cautiously.

insights.claim: The Houthi claim to target only Saudi-linked ships is functionally meaningless because a vessel carrying Saudi oil may be owned, operated, financed, insured or chartered by companies in several different countries and may be delivering to various destinations.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Ownership-based targeting rules do not ringfence risk: European and Chinese commercial interests, and marine underwriters, are exposed regardless of flag or nominal target set.
insights.quote: Houthi attacks on Saudi shipping therefore affect commercial interests far beyond Saudi Arabia, including in Europe and China.

insights.claim: Government-aligned forces withdrew rather than held as the Houthis pushed rapidly down the Red Sea coast, exposing coordination problems among a set of autonomous armed groups previously backed by different regional patrons with competing political ambitions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The anti-Houthi coalition is not a credible counterweight, so assume further territorial losses are possible without external intervention.
insights.locator: Houthi forces, who control most of western Yemen

insights.claim: Saudi attempts since early 2026 to bring anti-Houthi armed groups under a more coherent command structure have not erased years of fragmentation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Riyadh's proxy-consolidation project has already been tested and failed; Saudi options narrow toward direct action or negotiation.
insights.locator: Saudi attempts to bring them under a more coherent

insights.claim: The Houthis used the calm following the 2022 truce to recruit and mobilize personnel, improve domestic weapons production and expand missile and drone capabilities, and now hold more advanced capabilities than government forces in several areas.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Truces with the Houthis function as rearmament windows — a template that should discount the durability of any future ceasefire in the region.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the Houthis used the period of relative calm

themes.theme: Horn of Africa base cluster at risk

insights.claim: Djibouti sits roughly 20 kilometres from Perim Island, which the Houthis now reportedly control, placing a group with increasingly sophisticated drone, missile and maritime capabilities extremely close to a country hosting US, Chinese, French, Italian and Japanese military bases.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Five major powers' forward bases now fall inside Houthi drone range, raising the probability that an incident draws in a non-US power and broadens the conflict.
insights.quote: That places an armed movement with increasingly sophisticated drone, missile and maritime capabilities extremely close to a country that hosts US, Chinese, French, Italian and Japanese military bases.
insights.locator: Djibouti is just around 20 kilometres

insights.claim: Turkey and the United Arab Emirates also hold significant security and commercial interests in the Horn of Africa region affected by the Houthi advance.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Gulf and Turkish port and logistics assets around the Red Sea carry newly repriced political risk.
insights.locator: Other countries including Turkey and the United Arab Emirates

themes.theme: Trump's dilemma and the US-Houthi equilibrium

insights.claim: Washington and the Houthis have mutual incentives to avoid attacking each other even as the Houthis increase pressure on Saudi Arabia, because the May 2025 US truce spares Trump another costly Middle Eastern confrontation while the 2025 US air campaign caused the Houthis serious damage they do not wish to repeat.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The base case is continued US non-intervention despite Saudi attacks — do not assume automatic US escalation on Houthi headlines.
insights.quote: This creates a peculiar situation: Washington and the Houthis both have reasons to avoid attacking one another, even while the Houthis increase pressure on one of the US’s closest regional partners.
insights.locator: Washington and the Houthis both have reasons

insights.claim: The US-Houthi restraint equilibrium may break if the Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi territory, especially with even limited ground incursions across the border, which could pull Washington toward confrontation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A cross-border ground incursion is the specific tripwire to monitor for a regime change in oil and freight risk pricing.
insights.quote: That equilibrium, however, may not hold.
insights.locator: That equilibrium, however, may not hold

insights.claim: Houthi attacks into Saudi Arabia, including against energy infrastructure, have reportedly injured civilians and constitute an escalation that poses questions for Riyadh and its US ally.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Saudi upstream and export infrastructure is being struck again; watch Aramco facility disruption risk as a live oil supply variable.
insights.locator: The Houthis have also launched attacks into Saudi Arabia

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has vowed to respond to Houthi attacks on its territory and recently signed a mutual defence treaty with Turkey and Pakistan, but does not appear to have publicly called on either for assistance.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A new Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact is untested; its first invocation would be a major signal that Riyadh is diversifying away from US security guarantees.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia has vowed to respond

themes.theme: Humanitarian and economic cost inside Yemen

insights.claim: Almost 50,000 people have reportedly been displaced in Taiz alone since 3 September as a result of the renewed offensive.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Displacement at this pace signals the offensive is a sustained campaign, not a raid, and raises aid-funding and stabilization costs.
insights.quote: In Taiz alone, almost 50,000 people have reportedly been displaced since 3 September.

insights.claim: In Mocha, with health facilities collapsing or becoming inaccessible, local media report more than 240 pregnant women in the region face giving birth without access to functioning medical care.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Health-system collapse in newly captured territory foreshadows a humanitarian appeal against a backdrop of declining donor support.
insights.locator: In Mocha, the humanitarian consequences

insights.claim: Yemen enters this phase of war with divided institutions, an economy devastated by more than a decade of conflict and declining international humanitarian support, and further disruption to ports, roads and supply chains will drive up food, transport and fuel prices in a country heavily dependent on imports.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Import dependence plus port disruption means domestic inflation and famine risk compound quickly — a driver of further displacement and regional instability.
insights.locator: Lost beneath the geopolitical consequences

themes.theme: Siloed policy vs a unified adversary

insights.claim: Governments have treated Saudi-Houthi negotiations, maritime security, humanitarian access, Iran negotiations, the Yemeni government and Red Sea maritime security as separate issues, and that compartmentalized approach is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain now that the Houthis influence global shipping, energy markets, Gulf security, the Horn of Africa and the calculations of major powers.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Policy fragmentation implies slow, partial responses — meaning disruption persists longer than headline diplomacy suggests.
insights.locator: Governments have tended to treat Saudi-Houthi negotiations

insights.claim: Transactional containment fails because bilateral maritime security deals, localized negotiations and military strikes each operate in silos while the Houthis simultaneously function as a governing authority, an armed non-state actor, an Iranian regional ally and an increasingly important influence on maritime security.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Country-specific safe-passage arrangements offer only illusory protection; underwriting and routing decisions should not rely on them.
insights.quote: But these approaches operate in silos. The Houthis do not.
insights.locator: Recent developments should also challenge the idea

insights.claim: The Gulf Cooperation Council has not formulated a coherent Yemen policy because of disagreements between Gulf states and their different relationships with Yemeni factions, even though the Houthi advances now impact the entire GCC.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Absence of a GCC-wide position means no coordinated regional deterrent — a reason to assume escalation risk stays elevated.
insights.locator: For Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states in particular

insights.claim: Ignoring a crisis in Yemen does not contain it, and it is only a matter of time before it becomes an international crisis.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat current Red Sea disruption as an early stage rather than a plateau when sizing supply-chain and energy contingency plans.
insights.quote: Ultimately, ignoring a crisis in Yemen does not contain it. It is only a matter of time before it becomes an international crisis.
